'''Marilyn Esther Jacox''' (April 26, 1929 – October 30, 2013) was an American [[physical chemist]]. She was a [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]] (NIST) Fellow and Scientist Emeritus in the Sensor Science Division.<ref name=obit/><ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Thompson |first1=Warren E. |last2=Andrews |first2=Lester S. |last3=Irikura |first3=Karl K. |title=Marilyn Esther Jacox |journal=Physics Today |date=1 May 2014 |volume=67 |issue=5 |pages=65 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.2391 |bibcode=2014PhT....67e..65T |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

==Education==
Jacox was born in [[Utica, New York]], the daughter of Grant and Mary Jacox.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.bio-medicine.org/biology-news-2/Washington-area-chemist-wins-national-award-for-free-radical-research-5432-1|title=Place of birth|publisher=[[Bio-medicine]]|access-date=June 17, 2013}}</ref>

Jacox graduated summa cum laude with a degree in chemistry in 1951 from [[Syracuse University]], having attended the Utica campus, now [[Utica University]].  She received a Ph.D. degree in physical chemistry from [[Cornell University]] in September 1956, under the guidance of Prof. Simon H. Bauer. Jacox spent the next two years as postdoctoral research fellow in the chemistry department of the [[University of North Carolina]] in Chapel Hill, working with Prof. Oscar K. Rice.<ref>Lester Andrews, Bruce S. Ault, and [[Zakya Kafafi|Zakya H. Kafafi]], ''A brief Scientific Biography, Journal of Physical Chemistry A'', Vol. 104, No. 16, pp. 3431-3434 (2000).  The introduction of a Marilyn Jacox Festschrift issue.</ref>

==Career==
Following her postdoctoral work at University of North Carolina, Jacox became a Fellow in Solid State Spectroscopy at the Mellon Institute, where she began working on the spectroscopy of free radicals and other unstable chemical species trapped in [[Matrix Isolation|chemically inert cryogenic matrices]], an area that was to dominate her scientific work for the rest of her life. The first 15 years of this work was done in collaboration with [[Dolphus E. Milligan]], first at the Mellon Institute and, after 1963, at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] (later to be renamed National Institute of Standards and Technology). In the late 1950s, Jacox applied for positions at 75 universities, but only all-women's universities were interested. The NBS, however, was open to women (and people of color), leading women like Jacox and [[Anneke Levelt Sengers]] to do their research there.<ref name="chronicle">{{cite news|last1=Hovis|first1=Kathy|title=Alumna's bequest supports young female scientists |url=https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2015/10/alumnas-bequest-supports-young-female-scientists|access-date=July 4, 2017|work=[[Cornell Chronicle]]|date=October 26, 2015}}</ref> 

The Milligan-Jacox scientific collaboration only ended upon the death of Milligan in 1973.<ref>Andrews ''et al., ibid ''</ref> People noted that Jacox was scientifically active and highly productive up until her death.

Jacox received an [[Utica College]] Outstanding Alumnus Award in 1963 and five years later was awarded the Washington Academy of Sciences Award in Physical Sciences.<ref name="NIST Marilyn E. Jacox page">{{cite web|url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/div685/grp03/jacox.cfm|title=NIST Marilyn E. Jacox page}}</ref>  In 1970 she was awarded a U.S. Department of Commerce Gold Medal Award for her distinguished service. In 1973 she received the Federal Woman's Award from President [[Richard Nixon]]<ref>{{cite news|title=Richard Nixon: Remarks to Recipients of the Federal Woman's Award|url=http://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/ws/index.php?pid=4133|work=The American Presidency Project|publisher=University of California, Santa Barbara}}</ref> and the [[Samuel Wesley Stratton Award]] which she got from [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|National Bureau of Standards]].<ref name="NIST Marilyn E. Jacox page"/>

She was a member of the Inter−American Photochemical Society from 1978-79 on the Executive Committee level, and was an Election Committee member by 1980. In 1987 she received the ''40 Alumni of Achievement Award'' from [[Utica College]].<ref name="NIST Marilyn E. Jacox page"/> She was a member of [[Sigma Xi]] as President Elect from 1987−88, and as President from 1988-89. The same year she was awarded [[Ellis R. Lippincott Award]] by The Optical Society for her "seminal contributions in matrix-isolation spectroscopy research".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.osa.org/en-us/awards_and_grants/awards/award_description/ellislippincott/|title=Ellis R. Lippincott Award - The Optical Society osa.org. Retrieved 24 September 2019|last=|first=|date=|website=|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=}}</ref> In 2003, she was awarded the [[E. Bright Wilson Award in Spectroscopy]] by [[American Chemical Society]]. In the same year, she was awarded the first George C. Pimentel Award for her Advances in Matrix Isolation [[Spectroscopy]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://georgecpimentel.tripod.com/gcp-award.htm|title=Awards Named for George C. Pimentel|access-date=2015-12-12|archive-date=2004-05-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040527104011/http://georgecpimentel.tripod.com/gcp-award.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Jacox was a Fellow of both the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] and the [[American Physical Society]]. She was a reviewer for ''Chemical Intermediates'' from 1984−89, and for ''[[Journal of Chemical Physics]]'' from 1989–91. In 2007 she received another award and again from the Washington Academy of Sciences, for Distinguished Career in Science.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/div685/grp03/jacox.cfm|title=Biography of Dr. Marilyn Jacox|publisher=[[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]|access-date=June 15, 2013}}</ref>

An extensive interview with Jacox, recorded in 1998, is available in the NIST Digital Archives.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Beal |first1=Karma |title=Oral history interviews of Marilyn E. Jacox on February 11 and 18, 1998 |url=https://nistdigitalarchives.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16009coll2/id/293/rec/3 |website=NIST Digital Archives |access-date=28 September 2020}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
[[File:Marilyn E. Jacox with her camera.jpg|alt=Marilyn E. Jacox with her camera|thumb|Marilyn E. Jacox with her camera at the Fondation Beyeler in Basel, Switzerland]]
Marilyn E. Jacox researched and published the genealogy of her ancestors throughout her life,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Jacox |first=Marilyn E. |url=https://lccn.loc.gov/90168020 |title=The Jacox and Burlingame families of central and northern New York |date=1959 |publisher=M.E. Jacox |location=[Pittsburgh, Pa.]}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Jacox |first=Marilyn E. |url=https://lccn.loc.gov/93195480 |title=The Jacox and Burlingame families of central and northern New York: a history of the descendants of William and Sarah Jacockes of West Branch, Oneida County, New York |date=1993 |publisher=M.E. Jacox |location=[Gaithersburg, Md.]}}</ref> as well as being an ardent world traveller and photographer along the way.<ref name=":0" /> Friends and family were regularly treated to slide and video shows created by her.<ref name="obit" /> Otherwise, she kept herself busy attending photography, piano, and book clubs.<ref name=":0" />

==Death==
Jacox died, after a brief illness, on October 30, 2013, aged 84.<ref name=obit>{{cite news|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/washingtonpost/obituary.aspx?pid=167821788|title=Marilyn Jacox Obituary|newspaper= The Washington Post|publisher=[[Legacy.com]]|date=October 30, 2013|access-date=December 6, 2013}}</ref> She lived in [[Montgomery Village, Maryland]].

==Legacy==
Owing to the discrimination she experienced during her career, Jacox left $1.5 million to Cornell University's college of arts and sciences to provide scholarships for female undergraduate students majoring in science and math fields.<ref name="chronicle"/>
